chapter_theme: The swayamvara hall is built and adorned; the kings of Ayodhya, Hastinapura, Kundalapura, Varanasi, Suriyapura and Madurai arrive in state, and the prince Amitatejas outshines them all before the maiden is called in.

cast.role: the lord of kings who sits in the hall
the lord of the city who receives the guests
the dark-hued, discus-handed lord, taken to be Tivittan from the earlier chapters
the white-gleaming lord who arrives with him
the Vidyadhara lord of golden hue
the builders of the choosing hall
the one who proclaims the hour
the prince Amitatejas, who outshines the kings
the young women watching the assembly
the gentle maiden the king calls in to choose

1771.reading: In the golden city a walled grove-garden holds a shining hall; the lord of kings sits there and the city's own lord comes to receive him.
1771.nuance: The two lords are named only by their rank (the lord of kings; the lord of this city), so who is who rests on the earlier chapters.
1771.event: The city's lord goes out to receive the overlord of kings who has come to sit in the hall.

1772.reading: The dark-hued lord with the bright spear, the white-gleaming one, and the Vidyadhara of cool golden hue together make the earth blaze with their light.
1772.nuance: The three are given only by colour and kind (dark, white, a Vidyadhara of gold), so naming them rests on the story so far.
1772.event: Three lords arrive, each known by the hue of his body, and their brightness lights the ground.

1773.reading: As streets, courts and the rest fill on both sides, the sea-girt earth looks as if the world of the gods had come down.
1773.nuance: The simile makes the city a heaven set on earth, which prepares the pomp of the kings who arrive.

1774.reading: A pillared mansion with golden-crowned jewelled gate-towers and four doors shows fine jewel-work on every side.

1775.reading: Crystal slabs, coral pillars, golden vessels, silver bamboo-work and pearls of young light make the hall bright.

1776.reading: The white court of the hall, with its altars chilling the moonlight, seems to laugh at the four-faced Brahma's quarters.
1776.nuance: The poet sets the hall beside the Creator's own realm and says it laughs at it, a boast of the hall's worth.

1777.reading: The raised stages, five bow-lengths in measure, rise on gold pillars set with coral, with cloud-like hangings, as if the sky's stages had descended.

1778.reading: On balconies edged with emerald, thrones carried by young lions stand raised high.
1778.nuance: The thrones are held up by lion figures, the usual sign of royal seats.

1779.reading: Seats shaped like crocodile-thrones and swan-down cushions are set with gems.

1780.reading: Strings of pearls, crystal-bright garlands, gold wreaths and honeyed flower-ropes are hung through the hall.

1781.reading: Cotton seats are spread, flowers laid, and clouds of incense rise as though the hall were feasting the fierce sun.
1781.nuance: Honouring the sun-god with an incense feast turns the hall's preparation into a form of worship.
1781.event: Attendants spread seats and flowers and burn incense in the hall.

1782.reading: When the builders finish the hall of the choosing and spread couches in sandal shade, the musicians stand and play to say the work is done.
1782.event: Builders complete the choosing hall, and the musicians rise and begin to play.

1783.reading: At the auspicious hour a herald calls the kings to come and take their seats, conches sound, and the great drums roar as the kings appear.
1783.event: A herald calls the assembled kings to come in; conches and drums answer and the kings appear.

1784.reading: The lord of Ayodhya, born in the Ikshvaku line, enters the golden city with a splendid crown and strings of gems.
1784.event: The king of Ayodhya enters the city.

1785.reading: The king of Hastinapura, of the Kuru line, with arms like twin drums and shining with his own light, arrives.

1786.reading: The lord of Kundalapura, of the Nathavan line, with saffron-smeared shoulders and wreathed crown, enters with bees swarming over him.
1786.event: The king of Kundalapura enters the city.

1787.reading: The lord of Varanasi, of the Ugra line, rides in with a crested elephant, flashing earrings and women waving fly-whisks.
1787.event: The king of Varanasi rides into the city.

1788.reading: The lord of Suriyapura, born of the Hari line, comes forward on a mountain-like war-elephant, hair loose with its flowers, as the city praises him.
1788.event: The king of Suriyapura enters the city on an elephant.

1789.reading: The lord of Madurai, kin of the shining one the world praises, wearing the gem-necklace and sandal on his chest, enters as the city wishes him well.
1789.event: The king of Madurai enters the city.

1790.reading: The kings of the five great lines and others stand outside with their elephants and hosts, and the spear-bearers shine on golden seats.
1790.event: The kings take their seats, their armies waiting outside.

1791.reading: The prince Amitatejas, strong in battle and wearing the garland, goes in so brightly that the other kings' light is dimmed, as the moon is when it rises.
1791.nuance: The poet likens him to a young god and to the moon, so the verse sets up the contest by the one who dims the rest.
1791.event: Prince Amitatejas enters, outshining the assembled kings.

1792.reading: The young women's dark eyes fall on the handsome prince as bees fall on a maned elephant, and they leave the other kings they had come to the festival for.
1792.nuance: The eyes act before the bride does: the choice is anticipated in the gaze of the onlookers.
1792.event: The young women's eyes turn from the kings to the handsome prince.

1793.reading: When the kings are seated on their golden thrones, the discus-handed king calls the gentle maiden to come in, and drums and conches sound together.
1793.nuance: The calling voice is the king's, with the discus-hand; that he is Tivittan rests on the epithet and the earlier chapters.
1793.event: The king calls the maiden to come in and the drums and conches sound.

links.note: 1782 has the builders finish the hall and the musicians play; 1783 has the herald call the kings in at the auspicious hour.
links.teaches: The hall is finished before the hour is announced, so the festival's order moves from building to music to the kings' entry.

links.note: 1783 has the herald call the kings in and the drums sound; 1784 has the first king, of Ayodhya, enter.
links.teaches: The call is answered at once by named kings entering one after another, so the roll-call of kings is the proclamation's result.

links.note: 1791 has the prince outshine the other kings; 1792 has the young women's eyes leave the kings for him.
links.teaches: The brightness the poet claims for the prince is proved by where the onlookers look, not by the poet's word alone.

links.note: 1792 has the women's eyes already settle on the prince; 1793 has the king then call the maiden to come in.
links.teaches: The assembly's gaze is decided before the maiden is called, so her choice enters a room that has already leaned.

links.note: 1783 has conches and a great drum sound the hour of the kings' entry; Naladiyar 23 says the drums of a wedding hall can be the funeral drums of that very day.
links.teaches: The same drums that open a wedding hold the thought that joy and loss come under one roof.

gains.a: The festival scene gains the quatrain's warning that its drums do not guarantee the happy end it announces.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a hall with real drums and a gathering, set before the bride has chosen.

links.note: 1790 has kings of five great lines wait with elephants and hosts for the choosing; Naladiyar 21 says kings who rode elephants under moon-like umbrellas have been carried off and called dead.
links.teaches: The kings' show of force at the choosing is the same show that the quatrain says does not save a king.

gains.a: The roll of kings gains a measure by which their armies and elephants seem brief.
gains.b: The quatrain gains the sight of kings gathered in full strength and ready to be seen, at the moment the strength is displayed.

links.note: 1792 has young women's eyes fall on a handsome prince; Naladiyar 102 says beauty, youth, wealth and awe do not last.
links.teaches: The pull of the prince's looks is shown at full strength by the very verse that the quatrain would call short-lived.

gains.a: The moment of beauty's pull gains the quatrain's reminder that what draws the eye is passing.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case in which beauty actually moves a whole assembly, so its claim is set against real force.

source_issues: Verses 1784-1789 and 1791-1793 are printed in 8 half-lines in the source and joined into 4 lines; 1771, 1784 and 1785 and 1786 have pulli repairs flagged by the checker. Verse 1783 line 3 prints a bracketed (சு) in மாமுர(சு).
